lines.text: Research and study are the twin pillars of academic achievement, each requiring distinct skills and vocabulary. Study involves absorbing, understanding, and retaining knowledge through reading, note-taking, revision, and practice. Effective study strategies include active recall (testing yourself), spaced repetition (reviewing at increasing intervals), mind mapping (visual organisation of ideas), and the Pomodoro technique (focused 25-minute work blocks with breaks). Research goes further — it creates new knowledge through systematic investigation. The research process begins with formulating a research question, conducting a literature review, choosing a methodology, collecting data, analysing results, and drawing conclusions. Quantitative research uses numerical data and statistical analysis — surveys, experiments, and measurements. Qualitative research explores meanings, experiences, and perspectives through interviews, focus groups, case studies, and ethnography. Mixed methods combine both approaches. Primary research involves collecting original data; secondary research analyses existing sources. Peer review — where experts evaluate research before publication — ensures quality and credibility. Academic journals publish peer-reviewed articles; conferences allow researchers to present findings and receive feedback. Ethical research requires informed consent from participants, confidentiality, the right to withdraw, and approval from an ethics committee. The skills of critical reading, evidence evaluation, and logical argumentation developed through research extend far beyond academia — they are essential for navigating information in everyday life.
